note: Vol. I No. 33. THE CLEANEST PRINTING OF THE JULY 1 LETTER LIST in the month, again on page 1 column 2, and it settles a dozen names the readings of 1834-07-02 and 1834-07-09 had to bracket. THREE post-office lists stand in this issue — Chicago on page 1, Juliet on page 3 column 2, Plainfield on page 3 column 6. The town news is on page 3 and it is the busiest week of the month: a draw-bridge named as an address, an auction of public property at Fort Dearborn, and a dwelling in Wabansia described room by room.

Part 1 of 12 of the list of letters remaining in the Post Office at Chicago on 1 July 1834. THE HEADING is at lines 281-285, 'List of Letters' / '[R]EMAINING in the Post-Office at Chicago, I[ll]. July 1, 1834.', and JOHN S. C. HOGAN, P. M. signs it at line 659. THIS IS THE THIRD PRINTING of one list — the same list stands at page 3 column 2 of 1834-07-02 and page 1 column 2 of 1834-07-09 — and it is the BEST WITNESS of the three. What the earlier readings had to leave bracketed and this one prints whole: '[?] Adkins' is J. Adkins (302); 'Ara Brundaze' is Asa Brundage (321); 'I. C. Bristol' is R. C. Bristol (330); '[A]lf[r]ed Charchill' is Alfred Churchill (391); 'D. Pock' is D. Peck (398); '[uncertain: Rebecca Cleveland]' is Rebeca Clevland (401); 'sase Clark' is Isaac Clark (449); '[?]. M. Fish' is E. M. Fish (535); '[?]nn M. Gooding' is Ann M. Gooding (537); 'Robert F. Har[r]is' is Robert F. Haris (629). ONE NAME IS IN THIS PRINTING AND IN NEITHER OTHER: 'Levi Cady' at line 440. That is not a correction, it is a name the other two segmentations lost, and it is why a repeated list is worth reading again rather than cited back to the first witness. NORMALIZATION. Title case restored, recognition-class OCR corrected inside brackets, and a trailing numeral dropped from the reading because it is the count of letters held and not part of the name. A name whose printed form supports no reading keeps its whole self inside '[uncertain: …]'. Nothing here is corrected from the OTHER printings of this list: each claim stands on the lines it cites, the three readings are compared in this note and not merged, and where they disagree the disagreement is the record. A HAND COUNT, made against this column on 2026-08-28 and stated because the acceptance clause asks for one: page 1 column 2 runs 373 lines from 286 to 658; 298 of them are entries in the list and 75 are the heading, the signature, and one- and two-character slivers of the body column beside it. The extraction holds 298 entries — the same number, line for line. THE COUNT IS WHAT FOUND THE LAST EIGHT: the first pass of this claim held 290 and dropped 'stephen May', 'samuel Glugar', 'chandler Fi her', 'menry swartwout jr.', 'Jacob Guy 2', 'John Vafleet -', 'Elijah Wentworth sen.' and 'saml 11 ard' — every one of them a name whose surname was three letters long or whose line carried an uncertainty bracket. Counting the remainder rather than trusting the pass is what caught them, and the same count against 1834-07-09 found four more of the same shape.

claims.notes: A THIRD POST OFFICE'S LIST, and the whole of it: nine names and the postmaster, undamaged, on the same 1 July 1834 return as Chicago's and Plainfield's. Juliet — Joliet — is thirty-five miles south-west and these nine are NOT Chicago residents; `associated_places` says so on every entity. The list is printed complete in ten lines, which is what a small office's quarterly return looks like beside Chicago's two hundred and ninety, and that ratio is itself a fact about the size of the town. THREE LISTS IN ONE ISSUE — Chicago on page 1, this one, and Plainfield at page 3 column 6 line 4244 — all dated 1 July 1834 and all published together, which is the postal quarter and not a coincidence.

claims.notes: THE DRAW-BRIDGE IS AN ADDRESS. This is the only claim in the July run that places a business by the bridge, and it does it the way a town without street numbers does: by naming the road the bridge is at one end of, and where that road goes — to the oak woods and to Blue Island, south. For a reconstruction that has to decide what a road out of town looked like in 1835, a printed statement of where it went is worth more than the placement itself. THE STREET IS NOT NAMED and none is asserted; `street` stays null and the whole offset is the anchor. 'J. BATES, jr.' here against 'J. BATES, Auct.' at line 3054 and '[uncertain: Fae] BATES, Auct' in the issue of 1834-07-09: father and son, or one man read three ways, and no merge is declared — same surname, and the 'jr.' is exactly the kind of distinction the identity policy exists to preserve.

claims.notes: PUBLIC PROPERTY SOLD OUT OF A STORE HOUSE AT FORT DEARBORN — flour and 'a few other articles of public property' — which is a claim about the fort as a working depot in July 1834 and not only as a landmark. The words between 'Store House' and 'Fort Dearborn' are cut at line 3023-3025 and '[near]' is a supply of one preposition, bracketed; the line reads 'at the Store House' / 'Firt Dearborn, on t', so whether the store house is AT, NEAR or BELONGING TO the fort is not settled. THE DAY is '[19]th inst.', supplied from the Restorator sale advertised nine lines below at 3041 as 'On Saturday, the 19th inst. at 11 o'clock' — a different sale by the same auctioneer at the same hour, which is corroboration for the date and NOT for the two being one event. This column is interleaved with a leading article whose fragments ('Soldiers', 'nificence', 'the pros-', 'y guard') are excluded.

claims.notes: THE SAME PREMISES AS THE PREVIOUS WEEK'S SALE AND A FULLER DESCRIPTION OF THEM. On 1834-07-09 the notice read 'the unexpired lease of the Refectory, kept by J. A. Collett. Also the two [rooms ad]joining the rear' and that claim bracketed the word after 'two'. This printing says REFECTORY is RESTORATOR and that the two are not rooms but 'two small buildings adjoining the rear of the same' — so the premises are a principal building with two outbuildings behind it, and the furniture includes a complete cooking apparatus. THE SALE HAS BEEN PUT OFF: last week's notice gave 'Saturday the [?] inst.', which was the 12th, and this one is dated the 16th for Saturday the 19th. Both stand with their dates. 'Restorator' is the period word for an eating house and is kept rather than modernized.

claims.normalized: To Rent, or Lease. [A] CONVENIENT Dwelling House, in W[a]bansia, now occupied by Doctor Kimberl[y]. It has four rooms, with a kitchen, barn, an[d] garden attached to it. For terms, apply at t[he] office of Col. Hamilton. Chicago, July 16, 183[4].
claims.notes: A HOUSE DESCRIBED ROOM BY ROOM, WHICH ALMOST NOTHING IN THIS RUN IS: four rooms, a kitchen, a barn and a garden, in Wabansia, occupied by a doctor. For a reconstruction that has to decide what a dwelling of this town contained, a printed inventory of its parts is the strongest kind of evidence the papers give, and it is worth more than another storefront. WABANSIA is named as a place people live in — the same Wabansia the lithographic town map of 1834-07-02 includes (that issue's claim c052). THE TWO NAMES ARE CUT AT THE RIGHT EDGE and both are bracketed: 'Doctor Kimberl' has no final letter, and 'Col. Hamilton' is almost certainly the Rich'd J. Hamilton who is clerk of the Circuit Court and sells School Section lots in this same run — almost certainly is not a merge, and none is declared. E. S. Kimberly stands for the House of Representatives in the candidate list this paper prints weekly; that is a second Kimberly in the same issue and is NOT identified with the doctor.

claims.notes: THE VISITING DENTIST STAYS. On 1834-07-02 Kennicott advertised that he would 'practice the above profession in this place some four or five weeks' from an office at the Eagle Tavern, and that issue's claim c024 said in terms that ruling 3 would otherwise carry a four-week business to the scene date. Eight days later he prints that he is leaving for a short time and intends 'returning in the course of a few weeks, FINALLY TO LOCATE HIMSELF'. That is the contradiction resolving in the other direction, printed, and it is why the earlier note refused to set `contradicts`: the paper had not said it. NO ADDRESS in this notice, so the placement drops to `none`; the Eagle Tavern office belongs to the earlier claim and its own locator. The name is printed 'WH. I. KENNICOTT' where the earlier issue printed 'Wa. H. Kessicorr'; the two together support Wm. H. Kennicott and neither supports it alone.

claims.notes: THE INITIALS THE PREVIOUS ISSUE COULD NOT PRINT. On 1834-07-09 the Dearborn Street boot, shoe and leather store's display line was cut to '» TAYLOR' and its claim keyed the business on a bare surname. Here the same advertisement signs itself 'W. H. THE PLACEMENT is not repeated in the quoted lines and is carried by the earlier claim; `placement.class` here is `street_only` because Dearborn Street is what the standing ad gives and this half does not repeat the anchor. THE TRADE GROWS: last week the ad sold boots, this week it also makes them to order and warrants them.

claims.notes: ONE IMPRESSION OF THE STANDING LAKE STREET LAND-AGENCY CARD. The Democrat sets this advertisement, word for word the same, in every issue from 1834-05-14 to 1834-10-01 — twenty consecutive weeks, eighteen of which set the line ‘purchased and Sold, or by commi[s]sion’ recognisably (T-1051). The card is identified by its copy and not by its display line: the same trade (‘House and Land Agent’), the same offer of building lots in the town and the School Section, the same houses to let, and the same office on Lake street opposite Dr. Temple's. THIS IS ONE OF THE TWO IMPRESSIONS WHOSE COLUMN IS NOT A TESSERACT FALLBACK, and it is the reading T-0408 repaired the surname on: line 5527 sets '1* G. BLANCHARD,'. The SURNAME is therefore read here and not supplied. The FORENAME INITIAL IS NOT: '1*' is not 'W.', it is left unread in the normalization, and the record's 'W. G.' rests on identity.json's declared firm merge rather than on this line — T-0408's refusal of 'G. Blanshard' turns on exactly that initial and is untouched here. The column interleaves: 5528, 5529, 5531, 5533, 5535, 5538 and 5540 belong to the advertisement woven through, and the card's last two lines are set out of order (the address at 5541 before 'Enqure at the Office' at 5542), which the normalization unshuffles and the quote does not.
